title: What is in this image?
caption: Start with the same task as Part I: produce scores for possible answers.
notes:
What animal is this, and which parts made you decide?
Point to the face, fur, and silhouette before mentioning an architecture.

title: What can this patch tell us on its own?
caption: Part II: “bank” needed context. A patch can need context too.
notes:
Could this dark crop be fur, a shadow, or something else?
Reveal where it came from; keep pointing to the same crop.

title: We already know the operation. What changes?
caption: Carry the same objects and colours from Parts I–III into the photograph.
notes:
What stays the same when the input is a photograph?
Point to representation, contextual reading, and multiple head messages in the earlier examples.

title: What information could this patch borrow?
caption: The receiver stays a patch. Attention can bring it information from other locations.
notes:
Which visible regions might help interpret the dark crop?
Point to face, fur and nearby background; then trace messages back to the receiver.

title: Could a convolution use context too?
caption: A ViT changes the way spatial information is mixed.
notes:
Does attention have a monopoly on context?
Point to a local neighbourhood; describe how stacked convolutions widen the receptive field.

title: Cut on a grid; keep the pieces identifiable
caption: The grid can cut across a face, fur, and background.
notes:
Does each patch contain one whole object?
Reveal the grid, then match each enlarged crop back to its location.

title: What exactly is inside one RGB patch?
caption: Flattening rearranges numbers; it does not learn a representation.
notes:
How many numbers describe these four coloured pixels?
Read RGB inside each pixel, then concatenate the four triples in row order.

title: An image supplies the embedding rows
caption: Part I learned a vector for a character. Here, a shared linear layer maps each patch to a vector.
notes:
Do we need a different projection for every location?
Follow the four rows through the same operation. Locations enter separately.

title: How many weights turn pixels into a patch row?
caption: One learned projection is shared across locations. Positions enter afterwards.
notes:
Does doubling the number of patches double the projection parameters?
Trace one row through the matrix and bias; then reuse that operation for all patches.

title: Same patches. Can the answer change?
caption: Shrink the problem: four patches, two possible arrangements, every number visible.
notes:
How many filled and empty patches are in each image?
Reveal the second arrangement. Count two of each, then ask what changed.

title: Can a bag of patches tell these images apart?
caption: Predict what happens before we add position information.
notes:
What information was discarded when we made this bag?
Ask students to reconstruct the original layout; reveal that both layouts fit.

title: Turn one patch into four coordinates
caption: A shared patch projection; its last coordinate is a constant bias.
notes:
What is the mean of these four pixels?
Unroll P1 in row order. Compute the first coordinate, then reveal the full content row.

title: Can we calculate the entire patch projection?
caption: Each output coordinate is a dot product with one column of W_patch.
notes:
Which column computes ink, and which columns are zero?
Calculate all four coordinates, then add the bias.

title: Add where the patch came from
caption: The row and column coordinates distinguish locations. CLS starts as a learned summary row in a real ViT.
notes:
What distinguishes two identical filled patches now?
Point to the row and column coordinates. CLS is an extra row; it is not an image crop.

title: Where should a single image answer come from?
caption: Add a summary row, then let it read the same patch rows.
notes:
We have many contextual patch rows. How could we produce one image label?
Gather their messages into CLS; mention average pooling as another valid readout.

title: Should the top-left patch be forbidden to read the bottom-right?
caption: All image patches are observed before we predict the class. Standard ViT classification uses no causal mask.
notes:
What future information would leak from another patch in this task?
Compare a lower-triangular next-token mask with all-to-all image attention.

title: Could one patch mixture hide a useful distinction?
caption: Part III’s coat example returns: preserve more than one reading of the input.
notes:
What two kinds of information might help distinguish these layouts?
Point to row and column. Keep the same patches on both sides.

title: Which weights create the query, key and value?
caption: One input row; three separate learned projections. These worksheet weights are chosen for arithmetic.
notes:
What does each nonzero matrix entry copy or scale?
Follow the constant into Q, then ink and row into K and V.

title: Which features does this head compare?
caption: Part II again: the query and keys choose where to read.
notes:
What does multiplying this input by W_Q do?
Point to the fixed last coordinate supplying [1,1]. Then construct P1’s key.

title: One query; all five source weights
caption: Softmax normalizes across sources. The five weights sum to one.
notes:
Which keys give the same score?
Read the five rows, then reveal scores, exponentials, and normalized weights in that order.

title: Keep each weight beside its own value
caption: Multiply both value coordinates by the same source weight, then add down the columns.
notes:
What exactly does a source weight multiply?
Reveal values, then products. Add each coordinate before revealing the message.

title: Does the same attention weight mean the same message?
caption: The value vector determines what travels along an attention weight.
notes:
What do these two patches contribute to the ink coordinate?
Multiply both coordinates and compare the resulting messages.

title: A second head can choose a different mixture
caption: Part III: the same input rows, separate projections and a separate softmax.
notes:
Which patch now receives the greatest weight?
Point to P2’s ink and column, then reveal its score 2 and the new weights.

title: The second head sends its own message
caption: Multiply both value coordinates by the same source weight, then add down the columns.
notes:
What exactly does a source weight multiply?
Reveal values, then products. Add each coordinate before revealing the message.

title: What about the patch rows themselves?
caption: Every row receives a message. Our chosen queries make all five attention rows identical.
notes:
Do identical messages imply identical updated rows?
Compare the queries, then remind students that each residual starts from a different E row.

title: Join the messages; then combine their coordinates
caption: Concatenation preserves both messages. The output projection mixes them.
notes:
Which entries of W_O contribute to the first output coordinate?
Trace the first coordinate from both head messages through +1 and −1.

title: Keep the original row; add what it has read
caption: Part II’s residual update, followed by Part I’s class scores.
notes:
Does attention replace the original representation?
Add the vectors coordinate by coordinate. Then use the first updated coordinate for both logits.

title: Turn the two scores into an answer
caption: This softmax runs over class labels. Attention’s softmax ran over source rows.
notes:
What are the alternatives in this softmax?
Point to the two labels, then reveal the probabilities and the loss for the known answer.

title: Can we make the correct answer a little more likely?
caption: Freeze the worksheet and update a newly added two-number class bias with learning rate 0.5.
notes:
What sign should the gradient have for the correct class?
Compute p minus one-hot y, subtract half the gradient, then recompute the softmax.

title: Move the same patches, then remove position
caption: Change one thing at a time. Compare the two head messages and the class probabilities.
notes:
Will the class probabilities change if we permute patches without position information?
Take a prediction, choose Down the left, then turn positions off.

title: Put the familiar attention inside a full block
caption: Attention mixes information across rows. The MLP transforms each row separately.
notes:
Which operation communicates between patches, and which works on one row at a time?
Point to attention, then the MLP; trace both residual paths.

title: What does LayerNorm do to one row?
caption: Normalize across the coordinates of each token, independently of other tokens.
notes:
Which numbers participate in the mean and variance?
Use the four coordinates of one row; do not average across patches or the batch.

title: What can the MLP change without talking to another patch?
caption: Shared weights transform each row separately; the nonlinearity adds expressive power.
notes:
Where is information mixed here: between rows or between coordinates?
Trace one row through two linear layers and GELU, then add the residual.

title: What can a second block ask that the first could not?
caption: Every block receives the updated representations from the previous block.
notes:
Has the query in block two already seen other patches indirectly?
Trace the first residual update into the next block’s query projection.

title: Return to the photograph with a real ViT
caption: The pretrained model supplies learned representations and weights.
notes:
Which numbers change when we scale up?
Trace pixels, patch count, embedding width, heads, blocks, and the ImageNet label vocabulary.

title: How do image pixels become rows in code?
caption: A non-overlapping convolution implements the shared patch projection.
notes:
Why does this convolution produce exactly one output per patch?
Follow kernel size 2 and stride 2 across an 8×8 image.

title: Can we write attention in five lines?
caption: Softmax over the last axis means a distribution over source rows for each receiver.
notes:
Which axis must sum to one?
Match the source dimension in A to the row dimension in V.

title: What is the complete pre-LayerNorm block?
caption: MultiheadAttention includes concatenation and W_O. Both residual additions keep width D.
notes:
Where did the output projection go in this code?
Open the accompanying Block class: PyTorch’s attention module owns out_proj.

title: How does the full model produce image logits?
caption: Only the final readout selects CLS. Every transformer block processes all rows.
notes:
At what point do we discard the patch rows for classification?
Keep all 17 rows through both blocks, then select x[:,0].

title: Which call makes this model learn?
caption: Pass raw logits to cross_entropy. It combines log-softmax with the label loss.
notes:
Which line computes gradients, and which one changes the weights?
Distinguish backward from step. Point back to Part I’s learning loop.

title: Will it recognize a new noisy image?
caption: Randomize stripe location, intensity and pixel noise. Generate independent splits before training.
notes:
What would memorizing our original two clean images fail to demonstrate?
Compare noisy samples, then identify the roles of the three splits.

title: Does improvement carry over to unseen examples?
caption: Track training and validation during learning; reserve test images for the selected checkpoint.
notes:
What gap between these curves would worry you?
Read both curves at the same epoch, then explain minimum-validation-loss checkpoint selection.

title: What happens when a trained ViT loses position?
caption: Same generated splits and training recipe. Only the position mechanism is disabled.
notes:
Can any amount of training recover layout from the patch bag in this setup?
Reveal both test counts; connect the 50% result to paired permutation invariance.

title: Which pixels does the checkpoint actually receive?
caption: Show the exact 224×224 crop used for the measured prediction.
notes:
Are we feeding the original rectangular photograph directly to the network?
Match the original to the evaluation crop, then mention normalization.

title: The opening photograph goes through the actual model
caption: A measured prediction on this image. The worksheet explained the operations used inside.
notes:
What answer should the model assign to our opening image?
Reveal the saved top-three predictions. Compare the model’s label with the students’ original answer.

title: Does the same model recognize the other photograph?
caption: Run the identical preprocessing and learned weights on a Persian cat.
notes:
Do we change model weights when a different test image arrives?
Reveal the top three ImageNet labels and probabilities.

title: If our labels are “cat” and “dog”, what must change?
caption: Choose a task vocabulary and learn a suitable classifier from labelled training examples.
notes:
Is an ImageNet breed score already a fitted two-class Pets classifier?
Separate the checkpoint’s history, adapting a classifier, and running inference.

title: Do real heads put weight on the same places?
caption: Measured block 12, CLS query, heads 1–3. All three maps use the same colour scale.
notes:
Which similarities and differences can you see across heads?
Read the 14×14 source grid and the separately reported CLS self-weight.

title: Does the summary read the same way at every depth?
caption: Keep the image and CLS query identity fixed; compare two layers on one shared scale.
notes:
What changed between the two query representations?
Recall that later CLS queries already contain image-dependent context.

title: What if the receiver is a patch instead of CLS?
caption: Measured block 12, head 1. Query: patch row 7, column 5, counting from zero.
notes:
Which row of the attention matrix did we select this time?
Locate the purple receiver square, then read the source heatmap.

title: Does removing a region change the prediction?
caption: Four predetermined quadrant interventions; report the same target-class probability each time.
notes:
Which quadrant would you expect to affect this prediction most?
Collect predictions before revealing the measured bars.

title: What changes when the patch size is halved?
caption: At fixed image size, half the patch width gives four times as many patch rows.
notes:
Will attention-score count grow by four or roughly sixteen?
Count rows first, then square the total including CLS.

title: Can you predict the cost before changing the resolution?
caption: Count tokens, then count all query–key pairs.
notes:
What happens to the 197-token sequence at resolution 384?
Ask for a count, change the control, and compare with the prediction.

title: Your turn: which message arrives?
caption: Pause before revealing the weights and the weighted sum.
notes:
Can you calculate the softmax without a calculator?
Exponentiate ln 2 and zero; normalize two and one; multiply the value vectors.

title: Your turn: trace every important shape
caption: Keep patch count, embedding width and per-head width separate.
notes:
What is the difference between a patch’s 768 pixel values and the 64 embedding coordinates?
Let students write all shapes before revealing one line at a time.

title: Your turn: are these two shuffles equivalent?
caption: Distinguish moving image content from merely reordering the same positioned tokens.
notes:
Which shuffle changes what is located at the top left?
Track one patch and its position vector through each operation.

title: What can we do with these visual rows next?
caption: Keep the image representation; change the prediction task and training objective.
notes:
Which output would need one label, and which would need many spatial answers?
Trace CLS classification, then patch-level readouts and image–text interaction.

title: Can you now explain the whole photograph-to-answer path?
caption: The same attention story from Parts I–III, now attached to pixels we can inspect.
notes:
Which step is new, and which steps did we already know?
Ask students to narrate the computation from input to loss without reading equations.
